| Georgia O'Keeffe |  
| --- |  
| [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Georgia_O'Keeffe_MET_DP230868.jpg) O'Keeffe in 1932, photograph by Alfred Stieglitz |  
| Born | Georgia Totto O'Keeffe November 15, 1887 Sun Prairie, Wisconsin, U.S. |  
| Died | March 6, 1986 (aged 98) Santa Fe, New Mexico, U.S. |  
| Known for | Visual arts: painting, sculpture, photography |  
| Notable work | * _Black Iris_ * _Jimson Weed_ |  
| Movement | American modernism, Precisionism |  
| Spouse | Alfred Stieglitz ​ ​ (m.1924;died)​ |  
| Family | [Ida O'Keeffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ida_O'Keeffe "Ida O'Keeffe") (sister) |  
| Awards | National Medal of Arts (1985) Presidential Medal of Freedom (1977) Edward MacDowell Medal (1972) |
**Georgia Totto O'Keeffe** (November 15, 1887– March 6, 1986) was an American modernist painter and draftswoman whose career spanned seven decades and whose work remained largely independent of major art movements. Called the "Mother of American modernism", O'Keeffe gained international recognition for her paintings of natural forms, particularly flowers, hills and desert-inspired landscapes, which were often drawn from and related to places and environments in which she lived.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-cspan-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-:6-2) Although her work is often interpreted from a feminist perspective, she did not want to be seen as a "woman artist"; she wanted to be seen as an artist.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-4)

From 1905, when O'Keeffe began her studies at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, until about 1920, she studied art or earned money as a commercial illustrator or teacher to pay for further education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-EB-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-NCMA-6) Influenced by Arthur Wesley Dow, she began to develop her unique style through her watercolors during her studies at the [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Keeffe_at_the_University_of_Virginia,_1912%E2%80%931914 "O'Keeffe at the University of Virginia, 1912–1914") and, more dramatically, through the charcoal drawings she produced in 1915 that marked her move toward abstraction. Alfred Stieglitz, an art dealer and photographer, held an exhibit of her works in 1916.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-7) Over the next couple of years, she taught and continued her studies at the Teachers College, Columbia University.
In June of 1918 O’Keeffe was invited by Stieglitz to live and work in New York City and accepted this invitation as well as his offer to underwrite her year of painting in the city. She resigned from teaching at West Texas State to do so. Stieglitz and O'Keefe developed a professional and personal relationship that led to their marriage on December 11, 1924. In New York, O’Keefe created many reflections of her perception of the city through oil paint, charcoal, pastel, and watercolor. She looked back fondly at her pieces from this time, calling them ‘My New Yorks’. During this time, O'Keeffe created many forms of abstract art besides those of the city, including close-ups of flowers, such as the popular _Red Canna_ paintings.

O'Keeffe and Stieglitz lived together in New York until 1929, when O'Keeffe began spending part of the year in the Southwest, which served as inspiration for her paintings of New Mexico landscapes and images of animal skulls, such as _[Cow's Skull: Red, White, and Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cow's\_Skull:\_Red,\_White,\_and\_Blue "Cow's Skull: Red, White, and Blue")_ (1931) and [_Summer Days_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Days_(Georgia_O'Keeffe) "Summer Days (Georgia O'Keeffe)") (1936)_._ She moved to New Mexico in 1949, three years after Stieglitz's death in 1946, where she lived for the next 40 years at [her home and studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe_Home_and_Studio "Georgia O'Keeffe Home and Studio") or Ghost Ranch summer home in Abiquiú, and in the last years of her life, in Santa Fe.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-8) In 2014, O'Keeffe's 1932 painting _Jimson Weed/White Flower No. 1_ sold for $44,405,000—at the time, by far the largest price paid for any painting by a female artist.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-9) Her works are in the collections of several museums, and following her death, the [Georgia O'Keeffe Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe_Museum "Georgia O'Keeffe Museum") was established in Santa Fe.
Hilda Belcher, _The Checkered Dress_, 1907, Frances Lehman Loeb Art Center at Vassar College. The painting is likely a portrait of Georgia O'Keeffe.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-14)

Georgia O'Keeffe was born on November 15, 1887,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-Biography_channel-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-16) in a farmhouse in the town of Sun Prairie, Wisconsin.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-18) Her parents, Francis Calyxtus O'Keeffe and Ida (Totto) O'Keeffe, were dairy farmers. Her father was of Irish descent. Her mother's father, George Victor Totto, for whom O'Keeffe was named, was a Hungarian count who came to the United States in 1848.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-Biography_channel-15)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-roxana-19)

By 1929, she traveled to Santa Fe for the first time,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-59) accompanied by her friend Rebecca (Beck) Strand and stayed in Taos with Mabel Dodge Luhan, who provided O'Keeffe and Strand with studios.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-UNM-60) From her room she had a clear view of the Taos Mountains as well as the _morada_ (meetinghouse) of the _Hermanos de la Fraternidad Piadosa de Nuestro Padre Jesús Nazareno_, also known as the Penitentes.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-61) She subsequently visited New Mexico on a near-annual basis from 1929 onward, often staying there for several months at a time, returning to New York each winter to exhibit her work at Stieglitz's gallery.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-:62-62) O'Keeffe went on many pack trips, exploring the rugged mountains and deserts of the region that summer and later visited the nearby D. H. Lawrence Ranch,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-UNM-60) where she completed her now famous oil painting, _The Lawrence Tree_, currently owned by the Wadsworth Athenaeum in Hartford, Connecticut.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-63) O'Keeffe visited and painted the nearby historical San Francisco de Asís Mission Church at Ranchos de Taos. She made several paintings of the church, as had many artists, and her painting of a fragment of it silhouetted against the sky captured it from a unique perspective.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65)

In New Mexico, she collected rocks and bones from the desert floor and made them and the distinctive architectural and landscape forms of the area subjects in her work.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-Kort_p._170-39) Known as a loner, O'Keeffe often explored the land she loved in her Ford Model A, which she purchased and learned to drive in 1929. She often talked about her fondness for Ghost Ranch and northern New Mexico, as in 1943, when she explained, "Such a beautiful, untouched lonely feeling place, such a fine part of what I call the 'Faraway'. It is a place I have painted before ... even now I must do it again."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) O'Keeffe did not work from late 1932 until about the mid-1930s[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) due to nervous breakdowns.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-twolives-36) She was a popular artist, receiving commissions while her works were being exhibited in New York and other places.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-GOM_Summer_Days-66)

In 1933 and 1934, O'Keeffe recuperated in Bermuda and returned to New Mexico.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) In August 1934, she moved to Ghost Ranch, north of Abiquiú. In 1940, she moved into a house on the ranch property. The varicolored cliffs surrounding the ranch inspired some of her most famous landscapes.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) Between 1934 and 1936, she completed a series of landscape paintings inspired by the New Mexico desert, often with prominent depictions of animal skulls, including _[Ram's Head, White Hollyhock-Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ram's\_Head,\_White\_Hollyhock-Hills "Ram's Head, White Hollyhock-Hills")_ (1935) and _Deer's Head with Pedernal_ (1936). In 1936 she completed what would become one of her best-known paintings, _[Summer Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer\_Days\_(Georgia\_O'Keeffe) "Summer Days (Georgia O'Keeffe)")_.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-:12-67) Like _Ram's Head with Hollyhock_, it depicts desert scenery with a skull and vibrant wildflowers.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-GOM_Summer_Days-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-68)

*   Skulls and desert motif  
*   [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Georgia_O'Keeffe_Summer_Days_1936.jpg "Summer Days, 1936, oil on canvas, Whitney Museum of American Art")

*   [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:O'Keeffe_Georgia_Ram's_Head.jpg "Ram's Head, White Hollyhock-Hills, 1935, oil on canvas, Brooklyn Museum")

*
In 1938, the advertising agency N. W. Ayer & Son approached O'Keeffe about creating two paintings for the Hawaiian Pineapple Company (now Dole Food Company) to use in advertising.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-69)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-71) Other artists who produced paintings of Hawaii for the Hawaiian Pineapple Company's advertising include [Lloyd Sexton Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Sexton_Jr. "Lloyd Sexton Jr."), Millard Sheets, Yasuo Kuniyoshi, Isamu Noguchi, and Miguel Covarrubias.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-72) The offer came at a critical time in O'Keeffe's life: she was 51, and her career seemed to be stalling (critics were calling her focus on New Mexico limited, and branding her desert images "a kind of mass production").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-O'Keeffe's_Hawaii-73)

Source: https://bomackison.substack.com/p/georgia-okeeffe-and-her-art
Title: Georgia O'Keeffe and Her Art-- A Visit to the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum of Art in Santa Fe
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
At the Museum
Bright and sunny morning in Santa Fe, perfect for a walk in nature, but we had other plans. On our only full day in Santa Fe, we booked a morning visit to the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. There are priorities!
Let me take you on a brief tour of this amazing museum. (Italicized words from the O’Keeffe Museum.) What an incredible museum, with art displayed in such meaningful ways. I loved all the personal touches that only a museum with its focus on a single artist can render.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Bella Donna, 1939
_During her three-month stay in Hawaii in 1939, O’Keeffe created this painting, inspired by the flora she encountered. Though she gained acclaim in 1920s New York for her striking, enlarged flower paintings-such as Oriental Poppies (1927)-her time in Hawaii introduced new subjects and artistic perspectives. — O’Keeffe Museum of Art_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Ram’s Head, Blue Morning Glory, 1938
_O’Keeffe began visiting New Mexico in 1929 and, by 1931, started incorporating animal bones into her artwork. Later in the 1930s, she began juxtaposing these skull forms with her iconic flowers to visually powerful effects. —O’Keeffe Museum of Art_
“…you write about my flower…”
Georgia O’Keeffe, Blue Line, 1919, Oil on canvas.
When this painting was unveiled, there were a lot of scandalized people. Georgia found this situation amusing, claiming others’ personal interpretations about her up-close botanical art was “their problem, not mine.”
Georgia O’Keeffe, No. 17-Special, 1919, Charcoal on paper.
O'Keeffe's Style
_Circles and spirals appeared repeatedly in O’Keeffe’s early work, particularly in the 1910s; however, the motif all but disappeared from her work after Stieglitz’s death, in 1946. Later in life, in the 1970s, she returned to the theme, sometimes even using the same palette that had captured her attention years before. — O’Keeffe Museum_

Georgia O’Keeffe, Goat’s Horns with Blue, 1945, Pastel on paper.
_While many of O’Keeffe’s explorations of circular forms stemmed from her imagination, this 1945 pastel of a goat’s horn encircling a blue sky shows her interest in those found in the natural world as well. The angle at which O’Keeffe depicted the horn’s organic spiral recalls motifs used in her expressive early charcoal drawings of 1915. —O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Untitled (Abstraction Blue Circle and Line), 1976-1977, Watercolor on paper.
I love the colors, shapes and design of this untitled watercolor.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Patio Door with Green Leaf, 1956, Oil on canvas.
_Along with its large garden served by the acequia (irrigation ditch), O’Keeffe often cited this patio door as one of the primary reasons she wanted to own this adobe hacienda in the village of Abiquiú…_
_O’Keeffe’s decade-long attempts to negotiate a purchase were finally successful in 1945. O’Keeffe’s companion and assistant, Maria Chabot, coordinated the logistics of the transaction and oversaw the restoration of the property, which was completed in 1949. The patio door became the subject of more than twenty paintings and drawings by O’Keeffe. — O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Ram’s Skull with Brown Leaves, 1936, Oil on canvas.
_Beginning with her first trip to Northern New Mexico, O’Keeffe collected animal bones and skulls from the landscapes and used them as subjects in her paintings. She often depicted these animal remains against monochromatic or highly abstracted backgrounds, using distortions of scale to distance them from specific times and places. —O’Keeffe Museum_
Details of Ram's skull with Brown Leaves

_In 2025, environmental conditions in New Mexico once again played a part in the life of Ram’s Skull with Brown Leaves—historic flash floods breached the Roswell Museum of Art, which holds the painting in its collection. State and federal agencies aided staff and conservators with the recovery of nearly ten thousand artworks, including this painting. It is temporarily in the care of the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. —O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Black Hollyhock Blue Larkspur, 1930, Oil on canvas.
_During her stay at Mabel Dodge Luhan’s compound—a multi-dwelling residence bordered on two sides by Taos Pueblo land—O’Keeffe made frequent excursions to nearby locations, but also found artistic inspiration on the grounds. As she later recalled, “.. one day walking along the path [at Mabel’s] I picked a large blackish red hollyhock and some bright dark blue larkspur that immediately went into a painting-and then another painting.” —O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, The White Place, A Memory, 1943, Oil on canvas.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Red Hills and Sky, 1945, Oil on canvas.
So simple, right? And yet, studying this painting up close revealed an incredible amount of shading and color. It reminds me of the way I feel in desert—an awareness of simplicity, the light, the ever-expanding space into a forever emptiness.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Above the Clouds I, 1962-1963, Oil on canvas.
I have long admired O’Keeffe’s **Above the Clouds** series, but I am more familiar with the Above the Clouds V which hangs in a huge stairwell at the Art Institute of Chicago.
Even though Georgia is well-known for her love of the US Southwest, O’Keeffe also took inspiration in the aesthetic/architectural styles that she saw when she was a student at School of the Art Institute of Chicago.
She only spent one year at the Art Institute—leaving to recuperate from typhoid fever after one year—but she developed a loyalty to the institution, and left the art collection and personal photographs of her husband, Alfred Stieglitz, to the Institute after his death.

Georgia O’Keeffe, Untitled (Red and Yellow Cliffs), 1940, Oil on canvas.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Pelvis Series, Red with Yellow, 1945, Oil on canvas.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Spring, 1948, Oil on canvas.
Yousuf Karsh (1908-2002), Georgia O’Keeffe, 1956, Gelatin silver print.
On the morning we visited the museum, the place was packed with families, many with very young children. It was a “special event” day, and what an unexpected bonus that was, watching all the little kids interacting with their parents about the art they noticed. The kids were enthusiastic, curious, and full of energetic excitement. What a wonderful idea—introducing kids to the FUN that can be found in museums.
It’s been a decade since we were last in Santa Fe, and we’re hoping we don’t wait another decade before we visit again.
We didn’t stop at that one museum. After lunch, we returned to the square to visit a second museum, this one only a few steps away from O’Keeffe’s museum—the New Mexico Museum of Art. Bonanza street of art!
(Next up: A new-to-us artist, Gustave Baumann, at the New Mexico Museum of Art)

# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
By Medicine Man Gallery on May 31, 2023
Georgia O'Keeffe, Sky Above Clouds IV (1965) at the Art Institute of Chicago | Photo by Chadd Scott
On any short list of the best art museums in the United States, you will find the Art Institute of Chicago. No museum in the world has more instantly recognizable paintings: _Nighthawks, American Gothic_, Monet’s haystacks, Van Gogh’s bedroom, _A Sunday on La Grande Jatte_.
The best of the best.
Only.
The museum divides its permanent collection galleries into roughly 20 broad categories – Arts of Africa, Arts of China, Japan and Korea, Arms and Armor, Prints and Drawings, Impressionism, and so on. I made my first visit to the museum in April of 2023, not primarily looking for Western art – Western United States, not Western Civilization – but intrigued by the museum’s treatment of the genre after spotting one or two pieces here and there.
The Art Institute of Chicago’s focus is global and historic. It is what’s referred to as an “encyclopedic museum,” meaning, like an encyclopedia – remember those – it attempts to house a diverse assortment of objects highlighting 5,000 years of human creativity from around the world.
The Art Institute does not distinguish its Western material from its broadly American items unlike, say, the Denver Art Museum which specifically segregates its Western art onto a “Western American Art” floor. That makes sense. It’s been a long time since Chicago identified as a “western” city.
Walking through the galleries, it dawned on me, here in one of the greatest art museums in the world, with no effort being made to feature specifically Western art, in a non-western part of the country, whatever Western art made it up on the walls surely must be the finest examples of their kind.
So, what made the cut?
Georgia O’Keeffe didn’t simply make the cut, she was in the starting five. Across the entire collection, you might consider the stars of the Art Institute Monet, Van Gogh, Renoir and O’Keeffe. No artists have more or more prominent representation there.

# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
## Georgia O’Keeffe: Western Artist
I will sidetrack here briefly.
Why isn’t O’Keeffe more broadly accepted by the Western art establishment as a Western artist? Surely, she was more than a Western artist – she was one of the all-time great painters, an all-time great Modernist, an all-time great American artist – but she was also, surely, a Western artist. Anyone who doesn’t think so or consider her as such should ask themselves why?
She lived in New Mexico for nearly 40 years. She visited on extended trips for 20 years prior to that. She loved the West, she advocated for the West, she painted the West. Among her most famous artworks are pictures of cow skulls, ram skulls, mountains and deserts. She didn’t take her inspiration for these paintings from Manhattan.
Yet, to read the Western art magazines or listen to experts on Western art talk, O’Keeffe rarely comes up. This boggles my mind.
For a marginal genre within the broader art world like Western American art, those of us who love it should be co-opting and forwarding O’Keeffe at every turn. And Agnes Martin. And Marsden Hartley. And Richard Diebenkorn. And Raymond Jonson. And Diego Rivera.
Welcoming them under the Big Top tent of Western art would raise the profile of the entire genre and all of the artists within it.
We do this with Bierstadt and Moran. They didn’t exclusively paint the West and neither spent anywhere near the amount of time as O’Keeffe did there, but both are firmly entrenched within the Western art genre. Why not O’Keeffe?
I fear the answer may have to do with her gender, anything traditionally “Western” being overly confused and diseased by patriarchy and machismo.
Georgia O'Keeffe, Black Cross, New Mexico (1929) | Photo by Chadd Scott

# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
## Georgia O’Keeffe at the Art Institute
For O’Keeffe, born and raised in nearby Wisconsin, enrolling at the School of the Art Institute in 1905, her presence at the Art Institute of Chicago begins with the monumental _Sky Above Clouds IV_ (1965). And by monumental, I mean monumental: 8-feet high by 24-feet wide!
Painted when she was 77-years-old living in Abiquiu, New Mexico, the image portrays how she viewed the sky when traveling by plane. O’Keeffe was famous at this time, flying all over the country and world for events and exhibitions.
To me, this is a Western painting. Like O’Keeffe, not just a Western painting, but a Western painting also.
It’s vast, it’s landscape – or skyscape; it’s painted by a woman living and influenced by the West. Are these iconic clouds somehow less Western than Ed Mell’s or Tony Abeyta’s?
Ridiculous.
On my visit, the better part of an entire gallery in the “Arts of the America’s 1860-1950” section was devoted to O’Keeffe’s paintings and other artworks responding to O’Keeffe paintings. On display were bleached skulls and desert flowers and New Mexico landscapes – Western paintings.

# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
## Western Chicago
Representation of the West and western artists at the Art Institute of Chicago aside from O’Keeffe was scant, but noticeable to a keen eye. On view was a fantastic modern landscape painted in 1928 by Raymond Jonson, _Inscription Rock_. The scene comes from a sandstone headland now known as El Morro National Monument in New Mexico.
As mentioned previously, Jonson, and all of his Transcendental Painting Group colleagues, should be more fully embraced by the Western art genre. Just look at the work. It’s brilliant. It’s Western.
The prism of Western art should be broad, not narrow, to assure the genre’s continued relevance.
Hanging alongside the O’Keeffe’s was Marsden Hartley’s 1918-19 _The Last of New England – the Beginning of New Mexico._ Hartley was an easterner who spent 18 months in the Southwest during this time, but he “got” it, capturing the region like a native, a rare feat**.**
Two specifically Western art stalwarts had paintings on view in the Art Institute’s “Arts of the Americas, 1650-1910” section: Victor Higgins and Walter Ufer. Both pictures were representative of what they’re best known for.
Ufer’s _The Solemn Pledge: Taos Indians_ (1916) portrays a tender, sun-splashed scene of Native American ceremony. Ufer trained at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago.
Higgins not only studied at the School of the Art Institute, he taught there. His first visit to Taos was sponsored by Chicagoans supporting local artists. _Spring Rains_ (1924) depicts a bleached landscape with two Indigenous figures on horseback and a cow in the foreground around El Salto Peak in northern New Mexico. A cloud shadows the mountain as torrents of rain bring relief to the area.
Marsden Hartley, The Last of New England - The Beginning of New Mexico (1918-19) | Photo by Chadd Scott

# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
By Medicine Man Gallery on May 31, 2023
Georgia O'Keeffe, Sky Above Clouds IV (1965) at the Art Institute of Chicago | Photo by Chadd Scott
On any short list of the best art museums in the United States, you will find the Art Institute of Chicago. No museum in the world has more instantly recognizable paintings: _Nighthawks, American Gothic_, Monet’s haystacks, Van Gogh’s bedroom, _A Sunday on La Grande Jatte_.
The best of the best.
Only.
The museum divides its permanent collection galleries into roughly 20 broad categories – Arts of Africa, Arts of China, Japan and Korea, Arms and Armor, Prints and Drawings, Impressionism, and so on. I made my first visit to the museum in April of 2023, not primarily looking for Western art – Western United States, not Western Civilization – but intrigued by the museum’s treatment of the genre after spotting one or two pieces here and there.
The Art Institute of Chicago’s focus is global and historic. It is what’s referred to as an “encyclopedic museum,” meaning, like an encyclopedia – remember those – it attempts to house a diverse assortment of objects highlighting 5,000 years of human creativity from around the world.
The Art Institute does not distinguish its Western material from its broadly American items unlike, say, the Denver Art Museum which specifically segregates its Western art onto a “Western American Art” floor. That makes sense. It’s been a long time since Chicago identified as a “western” city.
Walking through the galleries, it dawned on me, here in one of the greatest art museums in the world, with no effort being made to feature specifically Western art, in a non-western part of the country, whatever Western art made it up on the walls surely must be the finest examples of their kind.
So, what made the cut?
Georgia O’Keeffe didn’t simply make the cut, she was in the starting five. Across the entire collection, you might consider the stars of the Art Institute Monet, Van Gogh, Renoir and O’Keeffe. No artists have more or more prominent representation there.
texts.4:
# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
## Georgia O’Keeffe: Western Artist
I will sidetrack here briefly.
Why isn’t O’Keeffe more broadly accepted by the Western art establishment as a Western artist? Surely, she was more than a Western artist – she was one of the all-time great painters, an all-time great Modernist, an all-time great American artist – but she was also, surely, a Western artist. Anyone who doesn’t think so or consider her as such should ask themselves why?
She lived in New Mexico for nearly 40 years. She visited on extended trips for 20 years prior to that. She loved the West, she advocated for the West, she painted the West. Among her most famous artworks are pictures of cow skulls, ram skulls, mountains and deserts. She didn’t take her inspiration for these paintings from Manhattan.
Yet, to read the Western art magazines or listen to experts on Western art talk, O’Keeffe rarely comes up. This boggles my mind.
For a marginal genre within the broader art world like Western American art, those of us who love it should be co-opting and forwarding O’Keeffe at every turn. And Agnes Martin. And Marsden Hartley. And Richard Diebenkorn. And Raymond Jonson. And Diego Rivera.
Welcoming them under the Big Top tent of Western art would raise the profile of the entire genre and all of the artists within it.
We do this with Bierstadt and Moran. They didn’t exclusively paint the West and neither spent anywhere near the amount of time as O’Keeffe did there, but both are firmly entrenched within the Western art genre. Why not O’Keeffe?
I fear the answer may have to do with her gender, anything traditionally “Western” being overly confused and diseased by patriarchy and machismo.
Georgia O'Keeffe, Black Cross, New Mexico (1929) | Photo by Chadd Scott
texts.5:
# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
## Georgia O’Keeffe at the Art Institute
For O’Keeffe, born and raised in nearby Wisconsin, enrolling at the School of the Art Institute in 1905, her presence at the Art Institute of Chicago begins with the monumental _Sky Above Clouds IV_ (1965). And by monumental, I mean monumental: 8-feet high by 24-feet wide!
Painted when she was 77-years-old living in Abiquiu, New Mexico, the image portrays how she viewed the sky when traveling by plane. O’Keeffe was famous at this time, flying all over the country and world for events and exhibitions.
To me, this is a Western painting. Like O’Keeffe, not just a Western painting, but a Western painting also.
It’s vast, it’s landscape – or skyscape; it’s painted by a woman living and influenced by the West. Are these iconic clouds somehow less Western than Ed Mell’s or Tony Abeyta’s?
Ridiculous.
On my visit, the better part of an entire gallery in the “Arts of the America’s 1860-1950” section was devoted to O’Keeffe’s paintings and other artworks responding to O’Keeffe paintings. On display were bleached skulls and desert flowers and New Mexico landscapes – Western paintings.
texts.6:
# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
## Western Chicago
Representation of the West and western artists at the Art Institute of Chicago aside from O’Keeffe was scant, but noticeable to a keen eye. On view was a fantastic modern landscape painted in 1928 by Raymond Jonson, _Inscription Rock_. The scene comes from a sandstone headland now known as El Morro National Monument in New Mexico.
As mentioned previously, Jonson, and all of his Transcendental Painting Group colleagues, should be more fully embraced by the Western art genre. Just look at the work. It’s brilliant. It’s Western.
The prism of Western art should be broad, not narrow, to assure the genre’s continued relevance.
Hanging alongside the O’Keeffe’s was Marsden Hartley’s 1918-19 _The Last of New England – the Beginning of New Mexico._ Hartley was an easterner who spent 18 months in the Southwest during this time, but he “got” it, capturing the region like a native, a rare feat**.**
Two specifically Western art stalwarts had paintings on view in the Art Institute’s “Arts of the Americas, 1650-1910” section: Victor Higgins and Walter Ufer. Both pictures were representative of what they’re best known for.
Ufer’s _The Solemn Pledge: Taos Indians_ (1916) portrays a tender, sun-splashed scene of Native American ceremony. Ufer trained at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago.
Higgins not only studied at the School of the Art Institute, he taught there. His first visit to Taos was sponsored by Chicagoans supporting local artists. _Spring Rains_ (1924) depicts a bleached landscape with two Indigenous figures on horseback and a cow in the foreground around El Salto Peak in northern New Mexico. A cloud shadows the mountain as torrents of rain bring relief to the area.
Marsden Hartley, The Last of New England - The Beginning of New Mexico (1918-19) | Photo by Chadd Scott

**Georgia Totto O'Keeffe** (November 15, 1887– March 6, 1986) was an American modernist painter and draftswoman whose career spanned seven decades and whose work remained largely independent of major art movements. Called the "Mother of American modernism", O'Keeffe gained international recognition for her paintings of natural forms, particularly flowers, hills and desert-inspired landscapes, which were often drawn from and related to places and environments in which she lived.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-cspan-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-:6-2) Although her work is often interpreted from a feminist perspective, she did not want to be seen as a "woman artist"; she wanted to be seen as an artist.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-4)
texts.1:
From 1905, when O'Keeffe began her studies at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, until about 1920, she studied art or earned money as a commercial illustrator or teacher to pay for further education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-EB-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-NCMA-6) Influenced by Arthur Wesley Dow, she began to develop her unique style through her watercolors during her studies at the [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Keeffe_at_the_University_of_Virginia,_1912%E2%80%931914 "O'Keeffe at the University of Virginia, 1912–1914") and, more dramatically, through the charcoal drawings she produced in 1915 that marked her move toward abstraction. Alfred Stieglitz, an art dealer and photographer, held an exhibit of her works in 1916.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-7) Over the next couple of years, she taught and continued her studies at the Teachers College, Columbia University.
In June of 1918 O’Keeffe was invited by Stieglitz to live and work in New York City and accepted this invitation as well as his offer to underwrite her year of painting in the city. She resigned from teaching at West Texas State to do so. Stieglitz and O'Keefe developed a professional and personal relationship that led to their marriage on December 11, 1924. In New York, O’Keefe created many reflections of her perception of the city through oil paint, charcoal, pastel, and watercolor. She looked back fondly at her pieces from this time, calling them ‘My New Yorks’. During this time, O'Keeffe created many forms of abstract art besides those of the city, including close-ups of flowers, such as the popular _Red Canna_ paintings.
texts.2:
O'Keeffe and Stieglitz lived together in New York until 1929, when O'Keeffe began spending part of the year in the Southwest, which served as inspiration for her paintings of New Mexico landscapes and images of animal skulls, such as _[Cow's Skull: Red, White, and Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cow's\_Skull:\_Red,\_White,\_and\_Blue "Cow's Skull: Red, White, and Blue")_ (1931) and [_Summer Days_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Days_(Georgia_O'Keeffe) "Summer Days (Georgia O'Keeffe)") (1936)_._ She moved to New Mexico in 1949, three years after Stieglitz's death in 1946, where she lived for the next 40 years at [her home and studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe_Home_and_Studio "Georgia O'Keeffe Home and Studio") or Ghost Ranch summer home in Abiquiú, and in the last years of her life, in Santa Fe.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-8) In 2014, O'Keeffe's 1932 painting _Jimson Weed/White Flower No. 1_ sold for $44,405,000—at the time, by far the largest price paid for any painting by a female artist.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-9) Her works are in the collections of several museums, and following her death, the [Georgia O'Keeffe Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe_Museum "Georgia O'Keeffe Museum") was established in Santa Fe.
Hilda Belcher, _The Checkered Dress_, 1907, Frances Lehman Loeb Art Center at Vassar College. The painting is likely a portrait of Georgia O'Keeffe.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-14)
texts.3: Georgia O'Keeffe was born on November 15, 1887,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-Biography_channel-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-16) in a farmhouse in the town of Sun Prairie, Wisconsin.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-18) Her parents, Francis Calyxtus O'Keeffe and Ida (Totto) O'Keeffe, were dairy farmers. Her father was of Irish descent. Her mother's father, George Victor Totto, for whom O'Keeffe was named, was a Hungarian count who came to the United States in 1848.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-Biography_channel-15)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-roxana-19)
texts.19: By 1929, she traveled to Santa Fe for the first time,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-59) accompanied by her friend Rebecca (Beck) Strand and stayed in Taos with Mabel Dodge Luhan, who provided O'Keeffe and Strand with studios.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-UNM-60) From her room she had a clear view of the Taos Mountains as well as the _morada_ (meetinghouse) of the _Hermanos de la Fraternidad Piadosa de Nuestro Padre Jesús Nazareno_, also known as the Penitentes.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-61) She subsequently visited New Mexico on a near-annual basis from 1929 onward, often staying there for several months at a time, returning to New York each winter to exhibit her work at Stieglitz's gallery.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-:62-62) O'Keeffe went on many pack trips, exploring the rugged mountains and deserts of the region that summer and later visited the nearby D. H. Lawrence Ranch,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-UNM-60) where she completed her now famous oil painting, _The Lawrence Tree_, currently owned by the Wadsworth Athenaeum in Hartford, Connecticut.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-63) O'Keeffe visited and painted the nearby historical San Francisco de Asís Mission Church at Ranchos de Taos. She made several paintings of the church, as had many artists, and her painting of a fragment of it silhouetted against the sky captured it from a unique perspective.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65)
texts.20: In New Mexico, she collected rocks and bones from the desert floor and made them and the distinctive architectural and landscape forms of the area subjects in her work.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-Kort_p._170-39) Known as a loner, O'Keeffe often explored the land she loved in her Ford Model A, which she purchased and learned to drive in 1929. She often talked about her fondness for Ghost Ranch and northern New Mexico, as in 1943, when she explained, "Such a beautiful, untouched lonely feeling place, such a fine part of what I call the 'Faraway'. It is a place I have painted before ... even now I must do it again."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) O'Keeffe did not work from late 1932 until about the mid-1930s[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) due to nervous breakdowns.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-twolives-36) She was a popular artist, receiving commissions while her works were being exhibited in New York and other places.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-GOM_Summer_Days-66)
texts.21: In 1933 and 1934, O'Keeffe recuperated in Bermuda and returned to New Mexico.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) In August 1934, she moved to Ghost Ranch, north of Abiquiú. In 1940, she moved into a house on the ranch property. The varicolored cliffs surrounding the ranch inspired some of her most famous landscapes.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) Between 1934 and 1936, she completed a series of landscape paintings inspired by the New Mexico desert, often with prominent depictions of animal skulls, including _[Ram's Head, White Hollyhock-Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ram's\_Head,\_White\_Hollyhock-Hills "Ram's Head, White Hollyhock-Hills")_ (1935) and _Deer's Head with Pedernal_ (1936). In 1936 she completed what would become one of her best-known paintings, _[Summer Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer\_Days\_(Georgia\_O'Keeffe) "Summer Days (Georgia O'Keeffe)")_.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-:12-67) Like _Ram's Head with Hollyhock_, it depicts desert scenery with a skull and vibrant wildflowers.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-GOM_Summer_Days-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-68)

*   [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:O'Keeffe_Georgia_Ram's_Head.jpg "Ram's Head, White Hollyhock-Hills, 1935, oil on canvas, Brooklyn Museum")

In 1938, the advertising agency N. W. Ayer & Son approached O'Keeffe about creating two paintings for the Hawaiian Pineapple Company (now Dole Food Company) to use in advertising.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-69)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-71) Other artists who produced paintings of Hawaii for the Hawaiian Pineapple Company's advertising include [Lloyd Sexton Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Sexton_Jr. "Lloyd Sexton Jr."), Millard Sheets, Yasuo Kuniyoshi, Isamu Noguchi, and Miguel Covarrubias.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-72) The offer came at a critical time in O'Keeffe's life: she was 51, and her career seemed to be stalling (critics were calling her focus on New Mexico limited, and branding her desert images "a kind of mass production").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-O'Keeffe's_Hawaii-73)

texts.0:
At the Museum
Bright and sunny morning in Santa Fe, perfect for a walk in nature, but we had other plans. On our only full day in Santa Fe, we booked a morning visit to the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. There are priorities!
Let me take you on a brief tour of this amazing museum. (Italicized words from the O’Keeffe Museum.) What an incredible museum, with art displayed in such meaningful ways. I loved all the personal touches that only a museum with its focus on a single artist can render.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Bella Donna, 1939
_During her three-month stay in Hawaii in 1939, O’Keeffe created this painting, inspired by the flora she encountered. Though she gained acclaim in 1920s New York for her striking, enlarged flower paintings-such as Oriental Poppies (1927)-her time in Hawaii introduced new subjects and artistic perspectives. — O’Keeffe Museum of Art_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Ram’s Head, Blue Morning Glory, 1938
_O’Keeffe began visiting New Mexico in 1929 and, by 1931, started incorporating animal bones into her artwork. Later in the 1930s, she began juxtaposing these skull forms with her iconic flowers to visually powerful effects. —O’Keeffe Museum of Art_
“…you write about my flower…”
Georgia O’Keeffe, Blue Line, 1919, Oil on canvas.
When this painting was unveiled, there were a lot of scandalized people. Georgia found this situation amusing, claiming others’ personal interpretations about her up-close botanical art was “their problem, not mine.”
Georgia O’Keeffe, No. 17-Special, 1919, Charcoal on paper.
O'Keeffe's Style
_Circles and spirals appeared repeatedly in O’Keeffe’s early work, particularly in the 1910s; however, the motif all but disappeared from her work after Stieglitz’s death, in 1946. Later in life, in the 1970s, she returned to the theme, sometimes even using the same palette that had captured her attention years before. — O’Keeffe Museum_
texts.1:
Georgia O’Keeffe, Goat’s Horns with Blue, 1945, Pastel on paper.
_While many of O’Keeffe’s explorations of circular forms stemmed from her imagination, this 1945 pastel of a goat’s horn encircling a blue sky shows her interest in those found in the natural world as well. The angle at which O’Keeffe depicted the horn’s organic spiral recalls motifs used in her expressive early charcoal drawings of 1915. —O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Untitled (Abstraction Blue Circle and Line), 1976-1977, Watercolor on paper.
I love the colors, shapes and design of this untitled watercolor.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Patio Door with Green Leaf, 1956, Oil on canvas.
_Along with its large garden served by the acequia (irrigation ditch), O’Keeffe often cited this patio door as one of the primary reasons she wanted to own this adobe hacienda in the village of Abiquiú…_
_O’Keeffe’s decade-long attempts to negotiate a purchase were finally successful in 1945. O’Keeffe’s companion and assistant, Maria Chabot, coordinated the logistics of the transaction and oversaw the restoration of the property, which was completed in 1949. The patio door became the subject of more than twenty paintings and drawings by O’Keeffe. — O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Ram’s Skull with Brown Leaves, 1936, Oil on canvas.
_Beginning with her first trip to Northern New Mexico, O’Keeffe collected animal bones and skulls from the landscapes and used them as subjects in her paintings. She often depicted these animal remains against monochromatic or highly abstracted backgrounds, using distortions of scale to distance them from specific times and places. —O’Keeffe Museum_
Details of Ram's skull with Brown Leaves
texts.2:
_In 2025, environmental conditions in New Mexico once again played a part in the life of Ram’s Skull with Brown Leaves—historic flash floods breached the Roswell Museum of Art, which holds the painting in its collection. State and federal agencies aided staff and conservators with the recovery of nearly ten thousand artworks, including this painting. It is temporarily in the care of the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. —O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Black Hollyhock Blue Larkspur, 1930, Oil on canvas.
_During her stay at Mabel Dodge Luhan’s compound—a multi-dwelling residence bordered on two sides by Taos Pueblo land—O’Keeffe made frequent excursions to nearby locations, but also found artistic inspiration on the grounds. As she later recalled, “.. one day walking along the path [at Mabel’s] I picked a large blackish red hollyhock and some bright dark blue larkspur that immediately went into a painting-and then another painting.” —O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, The White Place, A Memory, 1943, Oil on canvas.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Red Hills and Sky, 1945, Oil on canvas.
So simple, right? And yet, studying this painting up close revealed an incredible amount of shading and color. It reminds me of the way I feel in desert—an awareness of simplicity, the light, the ever-expanding space into a forever emptiness.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Above the Clouds I, 1962-1963, Oil on canvas.
I have long admired O’Keeffe’s **Above the Clouds** series, but I am more familiar with the Above the Clouds V which hangs in a huge stairwell at the Art Institute of Chicago.
Even though Georgia is well-known for her love of the US Southwest, O’Keeffe also took inspiration in the aesthetic/architectural styles that she saw when she was a student at School of the Art Institute of Chicago.
She only spent one year at the Art Institute—leaving to recuperate from typhoid fever after one year—but she developed a loyalty to the institution, and left the art collection and personal photographs of her husband, Alfred Stieglitz, to the Institute after his death.
texts.3:
Georgia O’Keeffe, Untitled (Red and Yellow Cliffs), 1940, Oil on canvas.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Pelvis Series, Red with Yellow, 1945, Oil on canvas.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Spring, 1948, Oil on canvas.
Yousuf Karsh (1908-2002), Georgia O’Keeffe, 1956, Gelatin silver print.
On the morning we visited the museum, the place was packed with families, many with very young children. It was a “special event” day, and what an unexpected bonus that was, watching all the little kids interacting with their parents about the art they noticed. The kids were enthusiastic, curious, and full of energetic excitement. What a wonderful idea—introducing kids to the FUN that can be found in museums.
It’s been a decade since we were last in Santa Fe, and we’re hoping we don’t wait another decade before we visit again.
We didn’t stop at that one museum. After lunch, we returned to the square to visit a second museum, this one only a few steps away from O’Keeffe’s museum—the New Mexico Museum of Art. Bonanza street of art!
(Next up: A new-to-us artist, Gustave Baumann, at the New Mexico Museum of Art)

# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
By Medicine Man Gallery on May 31, 2023
Georgia O'Keeffe, Sky Above Clouds IV (1965) at the Art Institute of Chicago | Photo by Chadd Scott
On any short list of the best art museums in the United States, you will find the Art Institute of Chicago. No museum in the world has more instantly recognizable paintings: _Nighthawks, American Gothic_, Monet’s haystacks, Van Gogh’s bedroom, _A Sunday on La Grande Jatte_.
The best of the best.
Only.
The museum divides its permanent collection galleries into roughly 20 broad categories – Arts of Africa, Arts of China, Japan and Korea, Arms and Armor, Prints and Drawings, Impressionism, and so on. I made my first visit to the museum in April of 2023, not primarily looking for Western art – Western United States, not Western Civilization – but intrigued by the museum’s treatment of the genre after spotting one or two pieces here and there.
The Art Institute of Chicago’s focus is global and historic. It is what’s referred to as an “encyclopedic museum,” meaning, like an encyclopedia – remember those – it attempts to house a diverse assortment of objects highlighting 5,000 years of human creativity from around the world.
The Art Institute does not distinguish its Western material from its broadly American items unlike, say, the Denver Art Museum which specifically segregates its Western art onto a “Western American Art” floor. That makes sense. It’s been a long time since Chicago identified as a “western” city.
Walking through the galleries, it dawned on me, here in one of the greatest art museums in the world, with no effort being made to feature specifically Western art, in a non-western part of the country, whatever Western art made it up on the walls surely must be the finest examples of their kind.
So, what made the cut?
Georgia O’Keeffe didn’t simply make the cut, she was in the starting five. Across the entire collection, you might consider the stars of the Art Institute Monet, Van Gogh, Renoir and O’Keeffe. No artists have more or more prominent representation there.

# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
## Georgia O’Keeffe: Western Artist
I will sidetrack here briefly.
Why isn’t O’Keeffe more broadly accepted by the Western art establishment as a Western artist? Surely, she was more than a Western artist – she was one of the all-time great painters, an all-time great Modernist, an all-time great American artist – but she was also, surely, a Western artist. Anyone who doesn’t think so or consider her as such should ask themselves why?
She lived in New Mexico for nearly 40 years. She visited on extended trips for 20 years prior to that. She loved the West, she advocated for the West, she painted the West. Among her most famous artworks are pictures of cow skulls, ram skulls, mountains and deserts. She didn’t take her inspiration for these paintings from Manhattan.
Yet, to read the Western art magazines or listen to experts on Western art talk, O’Keeffe rarely comes up. This boggles my mind.
For a marginal genre within the broader art world like Western American art, those of us who love it should be co-opting and forwarding O’Keeffe at every turn. And Agnes Martin. And Marsden Hartley. And Richard Diebenkorn. And Raymond Jonson. And Diego Rivera.
Welcoming them under the Big Top tent of Western art would raise the profile of the entire genre and all of the artists within it.
We do this with Bierstadt and Moran. They didn’t exclusively paint the West and neither spent anywhere near the amount of time as O’Keeffe did there, but both are firmly entrenched within the Western art genre. Why not O’Keeffe?
I fear the answer may have to do with her gender, anything traditionally “Western” being overly confused and diseased by patriarchy and machismo.
Georgia O'Keeffe, Black Cross, New Mexico (1929) | Photo by Chadd Scott

# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
## Georgia O’Keeffe at the Art Institute
For O’Keeffe, born and raised in nearby Wisconsin, enrolling at the School of the Art Institute in 1905, her presence at the Art Institute of Chicago begins with the monumental _Sky Above Clouds IV_ (1965). And by monumental, I mean monumental: 8-feet high by 24-feet wide!
Painted when she was 77-years-old living in Abiquiu, New Mexico, the image portrays how she viewed the sky when traveling by plane. O’Keeffe was famous at this time, flying all over the country and world for events and exhibitions.
To me, this is a Western painting. Like O’Keeffe, not just a Western painting, but a Western painting also.
It’s vast, it’s landscape – or skyscape; it’s painted by a woman living and influenced by the West. Are these iconic clouds somehow less Western than Ed Mell’s or Tony Abeyta’s?
Ridiculous.
On my visit, the better part of an entire gallery in the “Arts of the America’s 1860-1950” section was devoted to O’Keeffe’s paintings and other artworks responding to O’Keeffe paintings. On display were bleached skulls and desert flowers and New Mexico landscapes – Western paintings.

# Georgia O'Keeffe highlights Western artists at Art Institute of Chicago
## Western Chicago
Representation of the West and western artists at the Art Institute of Chicago aside from O’Keeffe was scant, but noticeable to a keen eye. On view was a fantastic modern landscape painted in 1928 by Raymond Jonson, _Inscription Rock_. The scene comes from a sandstone headland now known as El Morro National Monument in New Mexico.
As mentioned previously, Jonson, and all of his Transcendental Painting Group colleagues, should be more fully embraced by the Western art genre. Just look at the work. It’s brilliant. It’s Western.
The prism of Western art should be broad, not narrow, to assure the genre’s continued relevance.
Hanging alongside the O’Keeffe’s was Marsden Hartley’s 1918-19 _The Last of New England – the Beginning of New Mexico._ Hartley was an easterner who spent 18 months in the Southwest during this time, but he “got” it, capturing the region like a native, a rare feat**.**
Two specifically Western art stalwarts had paintings on view in the Art Institute’s “Arts of the Americas, 1650-1910” section: Victor Higgins and Walter Ufer. Both pictures were representative of what they’re best known for.
Ufer’s _The Solemn Pledge: Taos Indians_ (1916) portrays a tender, sun-splashed scene of Native American ceremony. Ufer trained at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago.
Higgins not only studied at the School of the Art Institute, he taught there. His first visit to Taos was sponsored by Chicagoans supporting local artists. _Spring Rains_ (1924) depicts a bleached landscape with two Indigenous figures on horseback and a cow in the foreground around El Salto Peak in northern New Mexico. A cloud shadows the mountain as torrents of rain bring relief to the area.
Marsden Hartley, The Last of New England - The Beginning of New Mexico (1918-19) | Photo by Chadd Scott

**Georgia Totto O'Keeffe** (November 15, 1887– March 6, 1986) was an American modernist painter and draftswoman whose career spanned seven decades and whose work remained largely independent of major art movements. Called the "Mother of American modernism", O'Keeffe gained international recognition for her paintings of natural forms, particularly flowers, hills and desert-inspired landscapes, which were often drawn from and related to places and environments in which she lived.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-cspan-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-:6-2) Although her work is often interpreted from a feminist perspective, she did not want to be seen as a "woman artist"; she wanted to be seen as an artist.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-4)

From 1905, when O'Keeffe began her studies at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, until about 1920, she studied art or earned money as a commercial illustrator or teacher to pay for further education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-EB-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-NCMA-6) Influenced by Arthur Wesley Dow, she began to develop her unique style through her watercolors during her studies at the [University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Keeffe_at_the_University_of_Virginia,_1912%E2%80%931914 "O'Keeffe at the University of Virginia, 1912–1914") and, more dramatically, through the charcoal drawings she produced in 1915 that marked her move toward abstraction. Alfred Stieglitz, an art dealer and photographer, held an exhibit of her works in 1916.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-7) Over the next couple of years, she taught and continued her studies at the Teachers College, Columbia University.
In June of 1918 O’Keeffe was invited by Stieglitz to live and work in New York City and accepted this invitation as well as his offer to underwrite her year of painting in the city. She resigned from teaching at West Texas State to do so. Stieglitz and O'Keefe developed a professional and personal relationship that led to their marriage on December 11, 1924. In New York, O’Keefe created many reflections of her perception of the city through oil paint, charcoal, pastel, and watercolor. She looked back fondly at her pieces from this time, calling them ‘My New Yorks’. During this time, O'Keeffe created many forms of abstract art besides those of the city, including close-ups of flowers, such as the popular _Red Canna_ paintings.

O'Keeffe and Stieglitz lived together in New York until 1929, when O'Keeffe began spending part of the year in the Southwest, which served as inspiration for her paintings of New Mexico landscapes and images of animal skulls, such as _[Cow's Skull: Red, White, and Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cow's\_Skull:\_Red,\_White,\_and\_Blue "Cow's Skull: Red, White, and Blue")_ (1931) and [_Summer Days_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Days_(Georgia_O'Keeffe) "Summer Days (Georgia O'Keeffe)") (1936)_._ She moved to New Mexico in 1949, three years after Stieglitz's death in 1946, where she lived for the next 40 years at [her home and studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe_Home_and_Studio "Georgia O'Keeffe Home and Studio") or Ghost Ranch summer home in Abiquiú, and in the last years of her life, in Santa Fe.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-8) In 2014, O'Keeffe's 1932 painting _Jimson Weed/White Flower No. 1_ sold for $44,405,000—at the time, by far the largest price paid for any painting by a female artist.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-9) Her works are in the collections of several museums, and following her death, the [Georgia O'Keeffe Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe_Museum "Georgia O'Keeffe Museum") was established in Santa Fe.
Hilda Belcher, _The Checkered Dress_, 1907, Frances Lehman Loeb Art Center at Vassar College. The painting is likely a portrait of Georgia O'Keeffe.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-14)

Georgia O'Keeffe was born on November 15, 1887,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-Biography_channel-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-16) in a farmhouse in the town of Sun Prairie, Wisconsin.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-18) Her parents, Francis Calyxtus O'Keeffe and Ida (Totto) O'Keeffe, were dairy farmers. Her father was of Irish descent. Her mother's father, George Victor Totto, for whom O'Keeffe was named, was a Hungarian count who came to the United States in 1848.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-Biography_channel-15)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-roxana-19)

By 1929, she traveled to Santa Fe for the first time,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-59) accompanied by her friend Rebecca (Beck) Strand and stayed in Taos with Mabel Dodge Luhan, who provided O'Keeffe and Strand with studios.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-UNM-60) From her room she had a clear view of the Taos Mountains as well as the _morada_ (meetinghouse) of the _Hermanos de la Fraternidad Piadosa de Nuestro Padre Jesús Nazareno_, also known as the Penitentes.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-61) She subsequently visited New Mexico on a near-annual basis from 1929 onward, often staying there for several months at a time, returning to New York each winter to exhibit her work at Stieglitz's gallery.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-:62-62) O'Keeffe went on many pack trips, exploring the rugged mountains and deserts of the region that summer and later visited the nearby D. H. Lawrence Ranch,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-UNM-60) where she completed her now famous oil painting, _The Lawrence Tree_, currently owned by the Wadsworth Athenaeum in Hartford, Connecticut.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-63) O'Keeffe visited and painted the nearby historical San Francisco de Asís Mission Church at Ranchos de Taos. She made several paintings of the church, as had many artists, and her painting of a fragment of it silhouetted against the sky captured it from a unique perspective.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65)

In New Mexico, she collected rocks and bones from the desert floor and made them and the distinctive architectural and landscape forms of the area subjects in her work.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-Kort_p._170-39) Known as a loner, O'Keeffe often explored the land she loved in her Ford Model A, which she purchased and learned to drive in 1929. She often talked about her fondness for Ghost Ranch and northern New Mexico, as in 1943, when she explained, "Such a beautiful, untouched lonely feeling place, such a fine part of what I call the 'Faraway'. It is a place I have painted before ... even now I must do it again."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) O'Keeffe did not work from late 1932 until about the mid-1930s[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) due to nervous breakdowns.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-twolives-36) She was a popular artist, receiving commissions while her works were being exhibited in New York and other places.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-GOM_Summer_Days-66)

In 1933 and 1934, O'Keeffe recuperated in Bermuda and returned to New Mexico.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) In August 1934, she moved to Ghost Ranch, north of Abiquiú. In 1940, she moved into a house on the ranch property. The varicolored cliffs surrounding the ranch inspired some of her most famous landscapes.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-ncmhf-65) Between 1934 and 1936, she completed a series of landscape paintings inspired by the New Mexico desert, often with prominent depictions of animal skulls, including _[Ram's Head, White Hollyhock-Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ram's\_Head,\_White\_Hollyhock-Hills "Ram's Head, White Hollyhock-Hills")_ (1935) and _Deer's Head with Pedernal_ (1936). In 1936 she completed what would become one of her best-known paintings, _[Summer Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer\_Days\_(Georgia\_O'Keeffe) "Summer Days (Georgia O'Keeffe)")_.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-:12-67) Like _Ram's Head with Hollyhock_, it depicts desert scenery with a skull and vibrant wildflowers.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-GOM_Summer_Days-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-68)

In 1938, the advertising agency N. W. Ayer & Son approached O'Keeffe about creating two paintings for the Hawaiian Pineapple Company (now Dole Food Company) to use in advertising.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-69)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-71) Other artists who produced paintings of Hawaii for the Hawaiian Pineapple Company's advertising include [Lloyd Sexton Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Sexton_Jr. "Lloyd Sexton Jr."), Millard Sheets, Yasuo Kuniyoshi, Isamu Noguchi, and Miguel Covarrubias.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-72) The offer came at a critical time in O'Keeffe's life: she was 51, and her career seemed to be stalling (critics were calling her focus on New Mexico limited, and branding her desert images "a kind of mass production").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_O'Keeffe#cite_note-O'Keeffe's_Hawaii-73)

Title: Georgia O'Keeffe and Her Art-- A Visit to the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum of Art in Santa Fe
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
At the Museum
Bright and sunny morning in Santa Fe, perfect for a walk in nature, but we had other plans. On our only full day in Santa Fe, we booked a morning visit to the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. There are priorities!
Let me take you on a brief tour of this amazing museum. (Italicized words from the O’Keeffe Museum.) What an incredible museum, with art displayed in such meaningful ways. I loved all the personal touches that only a museum with its focus on a single artist can render.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Bella Donna, 1939
_During her three-month stay in Hawaii in 1939, O’Keeffe created this painting, inspired by the flora she encountered. Though she gained acclaim in 1920s New York for her striking, enlarged flower paintings-such as Oriental Poppies (1927)-her time in Hawaii introduced new subjects and artistic perspectives. — O’Keeffe Museum of Art_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Ram’s Head, Blue Morning Glory, 1938
_O’Keeffe began visiting New Mexico in 1929 and, by 1931, started incorporating animal bones into her artwork. Later in the 1930s, she began juxtaposing these skull forms with her iconic flowers to visually powerful effects. —O’Keeffe Museum of Art_
“…you write about my flower…”
Georgia O’Keeffe, Blue Line, 1919, Oil on canvas.
When this painting was unveiled, there were a lot of scandalized people. Georgia found this situation amusing, claiming others’ personal interpretations about her up-close botanical art was “their problem, not mine.”
Georgia O’Keeffe, No. 17-Special, 1919, Charcoal on paper.
O'Keeffe's Style
_Circles and spirals appeared repeatedly in O’Keeffe’s early work, particularly in the 1910s; however, the motif all but disappeared from her work after Stieglitz’s death, in 1946. Later in life, in the 1970s, she returned to the theme, sometimes even using the same palette that had captured her attention years before. — O’Keeffe Museum_

Georgia O’Keeffe, Goat’s Horns with Blue, 1945, Pastel on paper.
_While many of O’Keeffe’s explorations of circular forms stemmed from her imagination, this 1945 pastel of a goat’s horn encircling a blue sky shows her interest in those found in the natural world as well. The angle at which O’Keeffe depicted the horn’s organic spiral recalls motifs used in her expressive early charcoal drawings of 1915. —O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Untitled (Abstraction Blue Circle and Line), 1976-1977, Watercolor on paper.
I love the colors, shapes and design of this untitled watercolor.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Patio Door with Green Leaf, 1956, Oil on canvas.
_Along with its large garden served by the acequia (irrigation ditch), O’Keeffe often cited this patio door as one of the primary reasons she wanted to own this adobe hacienda in the village of Abiquiú…_
_O’Keeffe’s decade-long attempts to negotiate a purchase were finally successful in 1945. O’Keeffe’s companion and assistant, Maria Chabot, coordinated the logistics of the transaction and oversaw the restoration of the property, which was completed in 1949. The patio door became the subject of more than twenty paintings and drawings by O’Keeffe. — O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Ram’s Skull with Brown Leaves, 1936, Oil on canvas.
_Beginning with her first trip to Northern New Mexico, O’Keeffe collected animal bones and skulls from the landscapes and used them as subjects in her paintings. She often depicted these animal remains against monochromatic or highly abstracted backgrounds, using distortions of scale to distance them from specific times and places. —O’Keeffe Museum_
Details of Ram's skull with Brown Leaves

_In 2025, environmental conditions in New Mexico once again played a part in the life of Ram’s Skull with Brown Leaves—historic flash floods breached the Roswell Museum of Art, which holds the painting in its collection. State and federal agencies aided staff and conservators with the recovery of nearly ten thousand artworks, including this painting. It is temporarily in the care of the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. —O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, Black Hollyhock Blue Larkspur, 1930, Oil on canvas.
_During her stay at Mabel Dodge Luhan’s compound—a multi-dwelling residence bordered on two sides by Taos Pueblo land—O’Keeffe made frequent excursions to nearby locations, but also found artistic inspiration on the grounds. As she later recalled, “.. one day walking along the path [at Mabel’s] I picked a large blackish red hollyhock and some bright dark blue larkspur that immediately went into a painting-and then another painting.” —O’Keeffe Museum_
Georgia O’Keeffe, The White Place, A Memory, 1943, Oil on canvas.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Red Hills and Sky, 1945, Oil on canvas.
So simple, right? And yet, studying this painting up close revealed an incredible amount of shading and color. It reminds me of the way I feel in desert—an awareness of simplicity, the light, the ever-expanding space into a forever emptiness.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Above the Clouds I, 1962-1963, Oil on canvas.
I have long admired O’Keeffe’s **Above the Clouds** series, but I am more familiar with the Above the Clouds V which hangs in a huge stairwell at the Art Institute of Chicago.
Even though Georgia is well-known for her love of the US Southwest, O’Keeffe also took inspiration in the aesthetic/architectural styles that she saw when she was a student at School of the Art Institute of Chicago.
She only spent one year at the Art Institute—leaving to recuperate from typhoid fever after one year—but she developed a loyalty to the institution, and left the art collection and personal photographs of her husband, Alfred Stieglitz, to the Institute after his death.

Georgia O’Keeffe, Untitled (Red and Yellow Cliffs), 1940, Oil on canvas.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Pelvis Series, Red with Yellow, 1945, Oil on canvas.
Georgia O’Keeffe, Spring, 1948, Oil on canvas.
Yousuf Karsh (1908-2002), Georgia O’Keeffe, 1956, Gelatin silver print.
On the morning we visited the museum, the place was packed with families, many with very young children. It was a “special event” day, and what an unexpected bonus that was, watching all the little kids interacting with their parents about the art they noticed. The kids were enthusiastic, curious, and full of energetic excitement. What a wonderful idea—introducing kids to the FUN that can be found in museums.
It’s been a decade since we were last in Santa Fe, and we’re hoping we don’t wait another decade before we visit again.
We didn’t stop at that one museum. After lunch, we returned to the square to visit a second museum, this one only a few steps away from O’Keeffe’s museum—the New Mexico Museum of Art. Bonanza street of art!
(Next up: A new-to-us artist, Gustave Baumann, at the New Mexico Museum of Art)

Source: https://github.com/WordPress/openverse/issues/5651
Title: Art Institute of Chicago
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
### Source API Endpoint / Documentation
API: https://api.artic.edu/api/v1/artworks (documentation: https://api.artic.edu/docs/). Full data dumps, updated nightly: https://github.com/art-institute-of-chicago/api-data

### Provider description
The Art Institute of Chicago is one of the largest art museums in the United States. Its collection covers about 5,000 years of art from around the world: paintings, prints, drawings, photographs, textiles, sculpture, architecture drawings and decorative arts. Its open access program releases images of works it believes to be in the public domain under CC0 (https://www.artic.edu/open-access/open-access-images). The API reports 62,119 public domain artworks (24 Oct 2026), for example "The Bedroom" by Vincent van Gogh: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/28560

### Licenses Provided
CC0 1.0 for images of public domain works (`is_public_domain: true` in the API). Collection data is CC0 1.0, except the `description` field, which is CC BY 4.0.

### Provider API Technical info
*   No API key. Anonymous requests are limited to 60 per minute per IP. The museum asks for a single thread and self-throttling.  
*   Public domain filter: `GET /api/v1/artworks/search?query[term][is_public_domain]=true` (Elasticsearch query DSL). `fields=` limits the response to the fields needed.  
*   Deep pagination is limited: the docs recommend the data dumps for result sets over 10,000 records. The dumps have the same schema as the API, so a full ingestion can read the dump and filter `is_public_domain` locally.  
*   Dated ingestion: `updated_at` can be filtered with a range query, but it changes for most records daily (37,897 public domain artworks had `updated_at` on or after 22 Oct 2026 when checked on 24 Oct), so a periodic full refresh from the dump looks more suitable than a date partitioned DAG.  
*   Images are served through the IIIF Image API 2.0: `https://www.artic.edu/iiif/2/{image_id}/full/843,/0/default.jpg` is the recommended size (200, 400, 600 and 843 pixel widths are cached; 1686 is allowed for public domain images). `thumbnail.width` and `thumbnail.height` give the full image size, and `thumbnail.alt_text` gives alt text.  
*   The museum asks for this caption with reproductions: "Artist. Title, Date. The Art Institute of Chicago."
Example (`/api/v1/artworks/search?query[term][is_public_domain]=true&limit=1&fields=id,title,artist_title,date_display,medium_display,dimensions,image_id,thumbnail,is_public_domain,updated_at,api_link`, `lqip` removed):

### Checklist to complete before beginning development
*   Verify there is a way to retrieve the entire relevant portion of the provider's collection in a systematic way via their API. (Nightly data dumps, or the search endpoint filtered on `is_public_domain` within the 10,000 record limit.) Verify the API provides license info (license type and version; license URL provides both, and is preferred). (`is_public_domain` per work; the response `info.license_links` points to CC0 1.0. There is no per-work license URL.) Verify the API provides stable direct links to individual works. (IIIF URL built from `image_id`.) Verify the API provides a stable landing page URL to individual works. (`https://www.artic.edu/artworks/{id}`.) Note other info the API provides, such as thumbnails, dimensions, attribution info (required if non-CC0 licenses will be kept), title, description, other meta data, tags, etc. (Title, artist, date, medium, dimensions, image size, alt text, classification and subject terms.)
